tool.name: PatchAnalysis
tool.summary: Finds the route through a corridor polygon that minimizes the patch-to-patch gaps an animal must cross moving between termini, using patches of good habitat as stepping stones, and reports the CRITICAL GAP -- the largest expanse of unsuitable habitat the species must cross in one push -- for every pair of termini. Distances are exact shortest paths inside the corridor polygon (a visibility graph -- no Spatial Analyst, no raster approximation), reported as geodesic meters. Outputs a polyline feature class of the gap crossings with named endpoints, lengths, and ranks. A modernized port of the CorridorDesigner Evaluation Tools' Patch Analysis. Needs no Spatial Analyst.
tool.usage:
WHAT THIS TOOL DOES. After you have built a corridor connecting wildland blocks, the next question is how well it serves the species. If some habitat inside the corridor is poor, the animal must cross expanses of unsuitable habitat -- but patches of good habitat can serve as stepping stones that break the journey into shorter pushes. Presumably you know the largest gap the species can cross (from foraging movements or juvenile dispersal distances); this tool tells you the largest gap the CORRIDOR will make it cross. For every pair of termini it finds the stepping-stone route that minimizes the longest single crossing, reports each route's segment lengths in decreasing order, and writes the crossings as polylines. If no patches are supplied (or none qualify), it simply reports the minimum distance needed to move between termini while staying inside the corridor.
WHY THE LONGEST GAP, NOT THE TOTAL DISTANCE. The route is the path between termini through a MINIMUM SPANNING TREE of the patch network (a variation on Kruskal's algorithm, exactly as in the original tool; see O'Rourke 2000, pp. 174-177). A minimum spanning tree path is the MINIMAX path: it minimizes the longest single edge traversed, not the total length. Ecologically that is the right question -- a corridor fails at its worst gap, however pleasant the rest of the journey. The tree property holds for every pair of nodes simultaneously, so ANY number of termini are analyzed in one run: this version generalizes the original's two-block limit, and termini lying in different disconnected strands of the corridor are reported as not connected.
EXACT VECTOR DISTANCES -- THE ORIGINAL'S BIG LIMITATION REMOVED. The original tool rasterized the corridor (600 cells on its long edge) and fell back on Spatial Analyst least-cost-path functions whenever a straight connector left the corridor, constraining paths to 45-degree increments and sometimes taking over an hour. This version computes constrained distances EXACTLY: a shortest path inside a polygon bends only at reflex (inward-pointing) corners of the corridor boundary, so the tool builds a visibility graph over those corners and finds true Euclidean shortest paths with Dijkstra's algorithm. No raster resolution parameter exists because no raster is involved; connectors bend precisely where the corridor makes them bend, and typical runs finish in seconds.
HOW THE PIECES ARE PREPARED, matching the original: patch polygons are clipped to the corridor, touching patches are merged, and a patch split between corridor strands becomes separate stepping stones. Corridor polygons traced from rasters routinely touch themselves at cell corners (technically invalid geometry); the tool repairs this automatically with a hair-thin buffer that also keeps those corner touches TRAVERSABLE, matching the original raster tool, whose 8-connected cost paths crossed diagonal cell touches -- so corner-touching corridor lobes count as connected, not as separate strands. Termini interior holes are ignored (routes connect their outer edges), and each terminus is clipped to the corridor -- a terminus that does not overlap the corridor at all is reported and left out. A connector that passes through a third polygon is discarded, because hopping through that polygon always gives smaller gaps (the discarded edge could never be on a minimax route). Polygons that touch (zero gap) are treated as connected with no crossing.
TERMINI AND THE NAME FIELD. Any polygon feature class can supply the termini -- most naturally this suite's Identify Termini Polygons output (its Block field is suggested automatically -- each Wildland Block is one terminus; the Category field there names the analysis surface, not the endpoints, so a multi-category termini layer should be filtered to one category first), but wildland block polygons or hand-drawn endpoints work equally well. Features sharing a name-field value are treated as ONE terminus (unlike the original, which required merging them first); with no name field, every feature is its own terminus, labeled by its object ID. At least two termini are required, and every pair gets its own route and critical-gap report.
PATCHES AND THE SELECTION EXPRESSION. The patch layer is optional and any polygon feature class works -- most naturally a Create Habitat Patches output, restricted with the SQL expression to the sizes that matter (for example Class_Name = 'Population patch', or GRIDCODE >= 3 for the original CorridorDesigner patch maps, matching the manual's Arizona ground squirrel example). Layer selections on every input are honored.
THE OUTPUT FEATURE CLASS holds one polyline per gap crossing on any route, in the corridor's own coordinate system: From_Name / To_Name (the terminus or stepping-stone patch at each end), Length_m (geodesic meters), Rank (1 = the longest crossing anywhere in the analysis), Used_By (the termini pairs whose route uses this crossing -- tree segments are often shared), and Crit_For (the pairs for which this crossing is the critical gap). The run messages list every route's segment lengths in decreasing order, as the original's report did. A path in a folder is written as a shapefile; in a geodatabase, as a feature class.
GEOGRAPHIC DATA AND LENGTHS. When the corridor is in a projected coordinate system, paths are computed in that system; when it is geographic (latitude-longitude), paths are computed in an azimuthal equidistant projection centered on the corridor -- built on the corridor's own datum, so no transformation is involved. All reported lengths are geodesic meters either way. Termini or patch layers on a DIFFERENT datum than the corridor are projected without a datum transformation (the dialog warns); for full control, project them to the corridor's coordinate system first.
THE SIMPLIFICATION TOLERANCE (Advanced). Corridor polygons traced from rasters (such as Least-Cost Corridor outputs) carry staircase boundaries with thousands of tiny corners. By default the boundary is simplified with a tolerance of 0.05% of the corridor's extent diagonal -- enough to strip staircase noise without moving the boundary at ecological scales -- before the visibility analysis. Because routes are computed against the simplified boundary, they can dip outside the exact original boundary by up to the tolerance where a wiggle was smoothed away -- cartographically invisible at the default. Set the tolerance to 0 to analyze the boundary exactly as supplied (slower), or raise it to speed up extremely detailed corridors.
EVERY OUTPUT KNOWS ITS PLACE IN THE CHAIN. The output is stamped with a machine-readable record (the same Supplemental Information mechanism the other corridor tools use) naming the corridor, termini, and patch sources, the parameters, every pair's route and critical gap, and the stepping stones used -- so the Corridor Analysis Data Report can re-tell the whole analysis later from the dataset alone.
ENVIRONMENTS. The output feature class honors the geoprocessing environments in the ordinary way; the analysis itself runs on the corridor's own coordinate system as described above.
CREDITS AND REFERENCES. The original CorridorDesigner Evaluation Tools are by Jeff Jenness (Jenness Enterprises), with the CorridorDesigner project by Dan Majka, Paul Beier, and Jeff Jenness; this ArcGIS Pro version is by Jeff Jenness. Please cite: Majka, D., J. Jenness, and P. Beier. 2007. CorridorDesigner: ArcGIS tools for designing and evaluating corridors. http://corridordesign.org. Minimum spanning trees and Kruskal's algorithm: O'Rourke, J. 2000. Computational Geometry in C, 2nd Ed. Cambridge University Press (https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511804120).

dialogReference.para: The corridor to analyze -- typically a Least-Cost Corridor polygon (or a Union Corridors output), but any polygon feature class or layer works. All features (or the selected ones) are treated together as the one corridor; a multipart or multi-feature corridor with disconnected strands is handled, with termini in different strands reported as not connected. Routes never leave this polygon.

The places the routes run between: an Identify Termini Polygons output, wildland block polygons, or any other polygon feature class. At least two termini are required; every pair of termini gets its own route and critical-gap report. Interior holes are ignored, and each terminus is clipped to the corridor (one that misses the corridor entirely is warned about and left out). A layer selection is honored.

param.name: name_field
param.displayname: Terminus name field (features sharing a value are ONE terminus)

dialogReference.para: The field naming the termini; features sharing a value are merged into one terminus, and the names label the route endpoints in the output and report. When the termini layer is an Identify Termini Polygons output, its Block field is suggested automatically (each Wildland Block is one terminus, labeled "Block 2", "Block 3", ...); do not group such a layer by Category, which holds the analysis-surface name and is the same on every row. Left blank, every feature is its own terminus, labeled by object ID.

Optional patches of good habitat that can serve as stepping stones -- typically a Create Habitat Patches output. Patches are clipped to the corridor, touching patches are merged, and each remaining piece is an available stepping stone (the route uses only the ones that help). A layer selection is honored. With no patches, the tool reports the plain shortest within-corridor distance between termini.

param.name: patch_where
param.displayname: Patch selection expression (e.g. only population-sized patches)

dialogReference.para: Restricts which patch polygons qualify as stepping stones -- typically a size or class rule, for example Class_Name = 'Population patch' on a Create Habitat Patches output, or GRIDCODE >= 3 on an original CorridorDesigner patch map. Applied on top of any layer selection.

The gap crossings of every route, as polylines in the corridor's coordinate system. Fields: From_Name and To_Name (the terminus or patch at each end), Length_m (geodesic meters), Rank (1 = longest crossing in the analysis), Used_By (the termini pairs routing over this crossing), and Crit_For (the pairs for which this is the critical gap). A path in a folder is written as a shapefile. The output carries the full analysis record for the Corridor Analysis Data Report.

param.name: simplify_tolerance
param.displayname: Corridor boundary simplification tolerance, meters (blank = automatic; 0 = none)

dialogReference.para: Raster-traced corridor boundaries carry staircase noise -- thousands of tiny corners that slow the visibility analysis without changing where routes really bend. Blank (the default) simplifies the boundary by 0.05% of the corridor's extent diagonal, which strips the staircase without moving the boundary at ecological scales. Enter 0 to analyze the boundary exactly as supplied, or a larger value in meters to speed up extremely detailed corridors.

scriptExample.title: Patch Analysis example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Finds the stepping-stone routes between all termini through a corridor, using only population-sized patches.
scriptExample.code:
import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages
arcpy.jenness.PatchAnalysis( r"C:\project\corridors.gdb\Corridor_Badger", # corridor polygon r"C:\project\corridors.gdb\Termini", # termini polygons "Category", # terminus name field r"C:\project\corridors.gdb\Badger_patches", # stepping-stone patches "Class_Name = 'Population patch'", # patch selection expression r"C:\project\corridors.gdb\PatchRoutes_Badger", # output connectors None) # simplification: automatic
